qs.q: A 3-year-old child presents with recurrent episodes of meningococcal meningitis. Further immunological evaluation is most likely to reveal a deficiency in which component of the immune system?
o: Deficiency in complement system components C5-C8
Deficiency in B-lymphocytes and total serum IgG
Deficiency in neutrophil oxidative burst function
Deficiency in primary splenic immune function
qs.e: Defects of the complement system, specifically components C5 through C8, are classically associated with recurrent meningococcal infections. Splenic dysfunction is instead primarily linked to pneumococcal, meningococcal, and H. influenzae sepsis rather than isolated complement pathways.

qs.q: An 8-month-old infant is diagnosed with bacterial meningitis. Before universal immunization programs, which pathogen was responsible for approximately 70% of bacterial meningitis cases in the first 5 years of life?
o: Listeria monocytogenes as a primary pathogen
Neisseria meningitidis as a primary pathogen
Streptococcus pneumoniae as a primary pathogen
Haemophilus influenzae type b as a primary pathogen
qs.e: Before universal vaccination, Haemophilus influenzae type b accounted for approximately 70% of bacterial meningitis cases occurring in the first 5 years of life. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis also cause meningitis but had different historical proportions.

qs.q: A child presents with meningitis following a basilar skull fracture with cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea. Which organism is most commonly associated with CSF leaks across a mucocutaneous barrier?
o: Pseudomonas aeruginosa invading cerebrospinal fluid
Streptococcus pneumoniae invading cerebrospinal fluid
Staphylococcus aureus invading cerebrospinal fluid
Listeria monocytogenes invading cerebrospinal fluid
qs.e: The risk of pneumococcal meningitis is specifically increased in children with congenital or acquired CSF leaks across mucocutaneous barriers such as skull fractures. Staphylococcus spp. are more commonly associated with dermal sinuses or CSF shunts.

qs.q: Which anatomical abnormality is specifically associated with an increased risk of staphylococcal, anaerobic, and Gram-negative enteric bacterial meningitis?
o: Cribriform plate cranial defect and fracture
Lumbosacral dermal sinus and myelomeningocele
Stapedial foot plate fistula of middle ear
Congenital cochlear aqueduct fluid anomaly
qs.e: Lumbosacral dermal sinus and myelomeningocele are specifically associated with staphylococcal, anaerobic, and Gram-negative enteric bacterial meningitis. Other options such as cribriform plate defects typically increase susceptibility to pneumococcal infections.

qs.q: An adolescent is evaluated for acute bacterial meningitis. Beyond the neonatal period, what are the three most common causes of bacterial meningitis in children older than one month of age?
o: Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus, and Escherichia coli
Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Neisseria meningitidis
Listeria monocytogenes, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Klebsiella pneumoniae
Neisseria gonorrhoeae, group B Streptococcus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae
qs.e: The three most common causes of bacterial meningitis in children older than one month are Haemophilus influenzae type b, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Neisseria meningitidis. Group B Streptococcus and E. coli are far more typical of neonatal meningitis.

qs.q: In regions of the African meningitis belt, which specific serogroup of Neisseria meningitidis accounts for the vast majority (80-85%) of major epidemics?
o: Neisseria meningitidis serogroup B
Neisseria meningitidis serogroup C
Neisseria meningitidis serogroup A
Neisseria meningitidis serogroup W
qs.e: In the African meningitis belt, serogroup A accounts for 80-85% of outbreaks. While other serogroups like B, C, X, Y, and W-135 cause invasive disease, serogroup A dominates epidemics in this region.

qs.q: An infant develops meningitis following the placement of an indwelling cerebrospinal fluid shunt. Which organisms are characteristically implicated in these shunt infections?
o: Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae
Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus spp., and Propionibacterium
Streptococcus pneumoniae and Listeria monocytogenes
Group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli
qs.e: CSF shunt infections increase the risk of meningitis caused by lower-virulence skin-colonizing bacteria like Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus spp., and Propionibacterium spp. Typical community-acquired pathogens like pneumococcus are less common in direct shunt colonization.

qs.q: During an autopsy of a child who died from acute bacterial meningitis, macroscopic examination reveals a purulent exudate distributed around the cerebral veins, sulci, and basal cisterns. Which diagnostic combination is standardly required to diagnose CNS infections ante-mortem?
o: Neuroimaging combined with cerebrospinal fluid testing
Complete blood count with differential and electroencephalography
Serum antibody titers and cranial nerve reflex testing
Blood cultures alone without cerebrospinal fluid analysis
qs.e: The diagnosis of CNS infection depends on a combination of brain imaging and testing of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) by culture, PCR, and serologic methods. Blood tests alone are insufficient to confirm meningeal involvement.

ai.summary: Meningitis is a severe infection of the meninges, the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord. It presents with fever, severe headache, and stiff neck, and can lead to rapid deterioration and serious complications.

sections.p: Meningitis is an inflammation of the meninges, typically caused by infection. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion supported by investigations, especially lumbar puncture, to identify the causative agent and inflammatory markers.
b: Key signs include fever, severe headache, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status.
In infants, irritability, poor feeding, and a bulging fontanelle may be present.

sections.p: Meningitis can range from mild to life-threatening. Severity is often assessed by the patient's clinical status, vital signs, and neurological examination, with rapid deterioration possible.
b: Rapid assessment of consciousness and haemodynamic stability is crucial.
Complications can significantly impact the patient's outcome and long-term prognosis.

sections.p: Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency. Viral meningitis is more common but usually less severe. Other causes include fungal, parasitic, and non-infectious inflammatory conditions.
b: Bacterial: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae.
Tuberculous meningitis: common in low-resource settings.
Viral: Enteroviruses, Herpes Simplex Virus.
Fungal: Cryptococcus (especially in immunocompromised individuals).

sections.p: Common symptoms include sudden onset of high fever, severe headache, photophobia, and a stiff neck. Altered mental status, from confusion to coma, can also occur. Seizures are a frequent complication.
b: Neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity) is a hallmark sign.
Photophobia (sensitivity to light) is common.
Altered mental status can range from mild confusion to coma.

sections.p: Lumbar puncture is essential for diagnosis, analysing cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for cells, protein, glucose, and Gram stain/culture. Blood tests and imaging may also be needed.

t.b: To identify the causative organism and inflammatory markers in CSF. Elevated white blood cells, protein, and low glucose suggest bacterial meningitis. Normal or slightly elevated cells and protein suggest viral meningitis. Culture confirms the specific pathogen.
To detect bacteraemia, which can indicate the source of infection or spread. Positive cultures help identify the pathogen and guide antibiotic choice.
To assess for signs of infection (e.g., elevated white blood cell count).
To rule out complications like brain abscess, hydrocephalus, or mass effect, especially if there are focal neurological signs or if lumbar puncture is contraindicated.

sections.p: Red flags include rapid deterioration of consciousness, seizures, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure. Complications are serious and can be permanent.
b: Seizures
Cerebral edema and herniation
Cranial nerve palsies
Hearing loss
Hydrocephalus
Neurological deficits (e.g., weakness, cognitive impairment)

sections.p: Prompt antibiotic therapy is critical for bacterial meningitis. Supportive care includes fluid management, fever control, and seizure management. Specific treatment targets the underlying cause.
b: Empirical antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) should be started immediately if bacterial meningitis is suspected.
Corticosteroids may be used to reduce inflammation and neurological sequelae.
Supportive care includes monitoring vital signs, managing seizures, and maintaining fluid balance.

sections.p: Follow-up is essential to monitor for complications and long-term sequelae. Prevention strategies include vaccination and prompt treatment of underlying infections.
b: Vaccination against common bacterial pathogens (e.g., Pneumococcus, Meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b) is key.
Prophylactic antibiotics may be given to close contacts of patients with meningococcal meningitis.
Early recognition and treatment of infections can prevent secondary meningitis.

sections.p: Several conditions can mimic meningitis, requiring careful differentiation based on clinical presentation and investigations.
b: Encephalitis
Subarachnoid hemorrhage
Brain abscess
Migraine
Cervical spine pathology

sections.p: Lumbar puncture results can be normal in early or partially treated meningitis. Imaging may be normal in early stages or if the pathology is subtle.
b: A normal white blood cell count in CSF does not exclude meningitis, especially in immunocompromised patients.
Fever may be absent in some cases, particularly in the very young or elderly.
Focal neurological signs can be absent despite significant intracranial pathology.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of meningitis?
faq.a: Bacterial meningitis is the most dangerous, with common causes including Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis. Viral meningitis is more frequent but usually less severe.
Yes, vaccination against key bacterial pathogens like Pneumococcus, Meningococcus, and Haemophilus influenzae type b significantly reduces the risk.

faq.q: What are the long-term effects of meningitis?
faq.a: Long-term effects can include hearing loss, learning disabilities, developmental delays, and neurological deficits, depending on the severity and cause of the infection.
